questions.title: Direction of proton movement through ATP synthase
questions.question: What is the direction of the movement of protons through ATP synthase?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Protons move matrix to intermembrane space through Complexes I, III and IV, which pump them out — the opposite direction to the one this option names, and not through ATP synthase itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cytoplasm is not a compartment of the mitochondrion; protons never leave the organelle to reach it, and this option confuses the intermembrane space with the cell's own cytoplasm.
explanations.C: Correct. The electron transport chain pumps protons out of the matrix into the intermembrane space, building an electrochemical gradient — the proton motive force. Protons can only return to the matrix through the F0 channel of ATP synthase, and it is this controlled return flow, from the intermembrane space back into the matrix, that drives the F1 head to synthesise ATP. Blocking this channel (oligomycin) stops ATP synthesis without stopping electron transport, which is how the two processes are shown to be chemiosmotically coupled rather than directly linked.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cytoplasm plays no part in this exchange; protons pumped into the intermembrane space return specifically to the matrix, not onward across the outer mitochondrial membrane into the cell.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that protons return to the matrix through ATP synthase, driven by the gradient the electron transport chain builds by pumping them out.

questions.title: Site of cyanide inhibition in the electron transport chain
questions.question: Cyanide inhibits electron transport chain at which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) is the target of rotenone, a different classic ETC poison, not cyanide.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) is inhibited by malonate; it is also the one complex that does not pump protons, and is not cyanide's site of action.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Complex III (cytochrome bc1) is the site antimycin A blocks, a separate inhibitor from cyanide acting one step earlier in the chain.
explanations.D: Correct. Cyanide binds the ferric iron of cytochrome a3 within cytochrome c oxidase, Complex IV, and blocks electron transfer to molecular oxygen at the chain's final step. With Complex IV inhibited, the whole chain backs up and oxidative phosphorylation stops even though oxygen is still delivered to the tissues in normal amounts — this histotoxic hypoxia is why cyanide poisoning kills rapidly, hitting the most oxidative-phosphorylation-dependent organs (brain, heart) first.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name Complex IV as cyanide's site of block in the electron transport chain.

questions.title: ATP yield from complete oxidation of acetyl-CoA in the citric acid cycle
questions.question: How many ATP molecules are produced on complete oxidation of acetyl CoA in the citric acid cycle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Three is far below the true yield; it ignores almost all of the electron-carrier output the cycle generates per turn.
explanations.B: Correct. One turn of the citric acid cycle, starting from acetyl-CoA, yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP (equivalent to ATP) directly. Using the standard P:O ratios of 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 ATP per FADH2 through oxidative phosphorylation, this comes to (3 × 2.5) + (1 × 1.5) + 1 = 7.5 + 1.5 + 1 = 10, which is conventionally rounded up to the commonly taught figure of 12 ATP using the older P:O ratios of 3 and 2 — the number examined here and in most undergraduate biochemistry teaching.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Six accounts for roughly half the true yield, undercounting the NADH and FADH2 generated across the cycle's four oxidative steps.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fifteen overstates the yield; no combination of the cycle's actual electron carriers and their P:O ratios reaches this figure for one acetyl-CoA.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State the ATP yield from complete oxidation of one acetyl-CoA through one turn of the citric acid cycle.

questions.title: Tissue in which the citric acid cycle does not operate
questions.question: Tricarboxylic acid cycle does not take place in which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hepatocytes are richly mitochondrial and run a full, active citric acid cycle as part of the liver's central metabolic role.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Osteocytes retain mitochondria and, like essentially all nucleated cells, carry out the citric acid cycle.
explanations.C: Correct. Mature erythrocytes extrude their nucleus and all organelles, including mitochondria, during maturation, leaving them entirely dependent on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP. Without mitochondria there is no matrix to house citric acid cycle enzymes and no electron transport chain to oxidise the NADH and FADH2 the cycle would otherwise generate, so the pathway simply cannot run in a mature red blood cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neurons are highly mitochondria-dependent, relying on oxidative phosphorylation (and therefore the citric acid cycle) for the large, continuous ATP supply their electrical activity demands.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the mature erythrocyte as the one nucleated-cell-derived tissue that cannot run the citric acid cycle, because it has no mitochondria.

questions.title: Major lipid-soluble antioxidant in the cell membrane
questions.question: Which vitamin is a major lipid soluble antioxidant in cell membrane?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vitamin A (retinol and its derivatives) is fat-soluble and important for vision and epithelial differentiation, but it is not the membrane's principal lipid-soluble antioxidant.
explanations.B: Correct. Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) sits within the phospholipid bilayer of cell membranes, where its chromanol ring donates a hydrogen atom to neutralise peroxyl radicals generated during lipid peroxidation. By breaking the chain reaction that would otherwise propagate through adjacent unsaturated fatty acids, vitamin E protects the structural integrity of membrane lipids from oxidative damage, making it the major lipid-soluble antioxidant in this compartment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vitamin D is fat-soluble and central to calcium and bone metabolism, but it has no significant direct antioxidant role in the cell membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin K is fat-soluble and essential as a cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, unrelated to membrane antioxidant defence.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name vitamin E as the major lipid-soluble antioxidant protecting cell membrane phospholipids from peroxidation.

questions.title: Heme-synthesis enzyme requiring pyridoxal phosphate as coenzyme
questions.question: Pyridoxal phosphate is necessary for the pathway of heme biosynthesis, which of the following enzymes requires pyridoxal phosphate as a coenzyme?

explanations.A: Correct. ALA synthase (delta-aminolevulinate synthase) catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of heme synthesis, condensing glycine and succinyl-CoA to form delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA). This condensation requires pyridoxal phosphate — the active form of vitamin B6 — as an essential coenzyme, which is why vitamin B6 deficiency or isoniazid therapy (which depletes pyridoxal phosphate) can produce a sideroblastic-type anaemia by starving this first committed step of the pathway.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ALA dehydratase (porphobilinogen synthase) condenses two molecules of ALA into porphobilinogen using a zinc-dependent mechanism, not pyridoxal phosphate, and is the enzyme classically inhibited by lead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Coproporphyrinogen oxidase, a mitochondrial enzyme later in the pathway, oxidatively decarboxylates coproporphyrinogen III without a pyridoxal phosphate requirement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ferrochelatase, the terminal enzyme of the pathway, inserts ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX to form heme, again without pyridoxal phosphate as a cofactor.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify ALA synthase as the pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent, rate-limiting enzyme of heme biosynthesis.

questions.title: Subcellular localisation of urea cycle enzymes
questions.question: Where are enzymes of the urea cycle localized?

options.A: Only in the mitochondria of the liver
options.B: Only in the cytoplasm of the liver
options.C: In the kidney mitochondria and cytoplasm
options.D: In the liver mitochondria and cytoplasm

explanations.A: Incorrect. Two of the five urea cycle enzymes (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase) are mitochondrial, but the remaining three are cytoplasmic, so the cycle is not confined to the mitochondria alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The first two steps of the cycle — carbamoyl phosphate synthesis and citrulline formation — happen inside the mitochondrial matrix, so the pathway is not purely cytoplasmic either.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The urea cycle is a liver-specific pathway; the kidney lacks a complete set of urea cycle enzymes (notably full carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I activity) and cannot synthesise urea de novo.
explanations.D: Correct. The urea cycle spans two compartments within the hepatocyte. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and ornithine transcarbamylase operate in the mitochondrial matrix, producing citrulline, which is then transported into the cytoplasm where argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinase and arginase complete the cycle, regenerating ornithine and releasing urea. This mitochondria-to-cytoplasm shuttle is why the cycle is described as split across both compartments of the liver cell specifically, not any other organ.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the urea cycle's enzymes are split between the mitochondria and cytoplasm of the liver, and no other organ runs the full cycle.

questions.title: Form of ammonia detoxification in the brain
questions.question: NH3 is detoxified in the brain in the form of which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ornithine is a urea-cycle intermediate confined to the liver and does not carry ammonia out of the brain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Asparagine is synthesised similarly (from aspartate) but is not the brain's route for exporting ammonia safely.
explanations.C: Correct. Astrocytes in the brain fix free ammonia onto glutamate using glutamine synthetase, forming glutamine — a non-toxic carrier that can be released into the circulation and delivered to the liver or kidney for further nitrogen handling. This route matters clinically because when hepatic ammonia clearance fails, rising blood ammonia crosses into the brain and drives excess astrocytic glutamine synthesis, whose osmotic effect contributes to the cerebral oedema of hepatic encephalopathy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alanine is the form skeletal muscle uses to export nitrogen via the glucose-alanine cycle, not the brain's own ammonia-detoxifying molecule.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the brain detoxifies ammonia as glutamine, distinct from muscle's alanine route.

questions.title: Phase 2 xenobiotic conjugation partner
questions.question: Phase 2 reaction of xenobiotic metabolism includes conjugation with which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulfate) is the sulfate donor for sulfation, a genuine but less common Phase 2 route than glucuronidation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acetyl-CoA donates an acetyl group in N-acetylation reactions, another real Phase 2 pathway, but again a minor one compared with glucuronidation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. SAM (S-adenosylmethionine) is the methyl donor for methylation reactions, a distinct Phase 2 conjugation pathway from glucuronic acid conjugation.
explanations.D: Correct. Glucuronidation is the most commonly occurring Phase 2 conjugation reaction: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases attach glucuronic acid to a drug, metabolite or endogenous compound (such as bilirubin), which usually increases its polarity and water solubility, allowing renal or biliary excretion. Its high capacity and broad substrate range make it the dominant Phase 2 route in xenobiotic detoxification, ahead of sulfation, acetylation or methylation.

questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: Name glucuronic acid conjugation (glucuronidation) as the most common Phase 2 xenobiotic conjugation reaction.

questions.title: Cause of acquired porphyria
questions.question: Porphyrias are rare group of diseases either hereditary or acquired. Which one of the following leads to acquired porphyria?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, from impaired collagen hydroxylation, and has no recognised role in porphyrin metabolism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) deficiency impairs coenzyme A synthesis; it is not linked to acquired disruption of heme synthesis.
explanations.C: Correct. Lead is a potent inhibitor of two heme-synthesis enzymes — ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase — by binding the sulfhydryl groups these enzymes depend on. This blocks heme production at two points in the pathway, causing accumulation of ALA and protoporphyrin and producing the acquired porphyria of lead poisoning, classically accompanied by microcytic anaemia, basophilic stippling of red cells and abdominal colic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cyanide poisoning blocks Complex IV of the electron transport chain, causing histotoxic hypoxia; it does not target heme-synthesis enzymes and is not a cause of acquired porphyria.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify lead poisoning as the classic acquired cause of porphyria, via inhibition of ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase.

questions.title: Cycle that recycles muscle lactate during prolonged fasting
questions.question: Fasting for more than 18 hours encouraged the process of gluconeogenesis, lactate formed in muscles can be utilized through which of the following cycles?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The glucose-alanine cycle carries nitrogen (as alanine, from transamination of pyruvate) from muscle to liver, not lactate itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The citric acid cycle oxidises acetyl-CoA within a single cell's mitochondria; it does not describe an inter-organ recycling loop for lactate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The urea cycle disposes of nitrogen as urea in the liver and has no role in recycling carbon skeletons such as lactate.
explanations.D: Correct. The Cori cycle carries lactate produced by anaerobic glycolysis in exercising muscle (and red blood cells, which always run anaerobically) to the liver, where gluconeogenesis converts it back to glucose, which is released into the blood and returned to muscle for further use. During prolonged fasting, this cycle becomes an important glucose-sparing route alongside amino-acid-derived gluconeogenesis, since it recycles carbon already in circulation rather than requiring new substrate.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name the Cori cycle as the route that recycles muscle-derived lactate to glucose via hepatic gluconeogenesis.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Bioenergetics

questions.title: Beta-oxidation product that can enter gluconeogenesis
questions.question: Which of the following products of triacylglycerol breakdown and subsequent B-oxidation may undergo gluconeogenesis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acetyl-CoA cannot be a net gluconeogenic substrate: the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction that forms it is irreversible, and its two carbons are lost as CO2 across one turn of the citric acid cycle before any net carbon could reach oxaloacetate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ketone bodies are themselves built from acetyl-CoA and are used as an alternative fuel by extrahepatic tissues; they share acetyl-CoA's inability to contribute net carbon to glucose synthesis.
explanations.C: Correct. Beta-oxidation of odd-chain fatty acids ends with a three-carbon residue, propionyl-CoA, rather than the two-carbon acetyl-CoA that even-chain fatty acids yield. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (a biotin-dependent enzyme) converts it to methylmalonyl-CoA, which is rearranged to succinyl-CoA — a citric acid cycle intermediate that enters before the irreversible pyruvate dehydrogenase step and so can be drawn off to oxaloacetate and on into gluconeogenesis. This is the specific reason odd-chain (but not even-chain) fatty acid breakdown is glucogenic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Amino acids are correctly glucogenic in general, but they are products of protein catabolism, not products of triacylglycerol breakdown and beta-oxidation, so this option does not answer what the stem asks.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Explain why propionyl-CoA, from odd-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation, is glucogenic via succinyl-CoA, while acetyl-CoA is not.

questions.title: Net ATP yield of anaerobic glycolysis
questions.question: Glycolysis may occur anaerobically. What is the energy yield from each molecule of glucose in anaerobic glycolysis?

explanations.A: Correct. Anaerobic glycolysis invests 2 ATP in the preparatory phase (hexokinase and phosphofructokinase steps) and generates 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation in the payoff phase (phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps, each occurring twice per glucose), for a net yield of 2 ATP per glucose. The NADH produced cannot be oxidised through the electron transport chain without oxygen, so it is instead reoxidised to NAD+ by converting pyruvate to lactate (lactate dehydrogenase), which regenerates the NAD+ glycolysis needs to continue but adds no further ATP.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Six ATP would require electron-transport-chain oxidation of the NADH generated, which anaerobic conditions specifically prevent.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Eight ATP overstates even the aerobic glycolytic yield before the citric acid cycle and full oxidative phosphorylation are added.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Twelve ATP corresponds roughly to the yield of one full turn of the citric acid cycle from acetyl-CoA, not to glycolysis itself, aerobic or anaerobic.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that anaerobic glycolysis yields a net 2 ATP per glucose, with NADH reoxidised via lactate formation rather than the electron transport chain.

questions.title: Enzyme catalysing phosphorolysis of the alpha-1,4 bond in glycogenolysis
questions.question: Which one of the following enzymes of glycogenolysis catalyzes phosphorolysis of the a-1-4 glycosidic linkage of glycogen?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glycogen synthase builds glycogen, adding glucose units via alpha-1,4 bonds during synthesis — the opposite reaction to the breakdown this question describes.
explanations.B: Correct. Glycogen phosphorylase catalyses phosphorolysis — cleavage by inorganic phosphate rather than water — of the alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds linking glucose units in glycogen's linear chains, releasing glucose-1-phosphate one unit at a time from the non-reducing ends. This phosphorolytic (rather than hydrolytic) mechanism is energetically efficient, since the released sugar is already phosphorylated and can enter glycolysis without spending an additional ATP on the hexokinase step.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A phosphatase (such as the one that removes the phosphate from glucose-6-phosphate in the liver) acts later, freeing glucose for release into the blood, not on the alpha-1,4 bonds of glycogen itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Debranching enzyme acts specifically on the alpha-1,6 branch points of glycogen, transferring and then hydrolysing residues there — a different bond from the alpha-1,4 linkage this question asks about.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify glycogen phosphorylase as the enzyme that phosphorolyses the alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds of glycogen during glycogenolysis.

questions.title: Muscle biopsy finding in McArdle disease
questions.question: A 25-year-old man suffered from increased fatigue and developed muscle pains and cramps when playing outfield for his office softball team. His physician suspected McArdle disease. A diagnostic muscle biopsy is likely to show which of the the following?

options.A: Increased normal glycogen with decreased hexokinase
options.B: Increased normal glycogen with deficient glycogen synthase
options.C: Increased normal glycogen with deficient phosphorylase
options.D: Decreased muscle glycogen with decreased glycogen synthase

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hexokinase deficiency would impair glucose entry into glycolysis broadly, but this is not McArdle disease's defect and does not match its glycogen-storage picture.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Deficient glycogen synthase would cause reduced, not increased, glycogen accumulation, since it is the enzyme that builds glycogen in the first place.
explanations.C: Correct. McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V) is caused by deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase). Because glycogen can still be synthesised normally but cannot be broken down, muscle biopsy shows an increased amount of structurally normal glycogen, and the enzyme block prevents glucose release from glycogen during exercise, producing exercise intolerance, cramps and myalgia — exactly the picture in this softball player.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Decreased glycogen with decreased glycogen synthase describes a synthesis defect, the reverse pattern from the accumulation seen when breakdown, not synthesis, is blocked.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify McArdle disease as myophosphorylase deficiency, producing increased structurally normal muscle glycogen that cannot be mobilised during exercise.

questions.title: Amino acid excluded from transamination
questions.question: Which of the following amino acids do not participate in transamination?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glutamic acid is central to transamination — it is the universal amino-group acceptor/donor that essentially every aminotransferase reaction funnels through.
explanations.B: Correct. Proline is an imino acid: its side chain cyclises back onto its own nitrogen, forming a secondary amine within a ring rather than a free primary alpha-amino group. Because standard aminotransferases require a free alpha-amino group to transfer, proline (along with lysine, threonine and hydroxyproline) cannot undergo the typical transamination reaction and instead follows separate degradation routes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Serine readily undergoes transamination, and can also be interconverted with glycine and feed into one-carbon metabolism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alanine is a classic transamination substrate/product, central to the glucose-alanine cycle that carries nitrogen from muscle to liver.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify proline as an amino acid excluded from standard transamination because it lacks a free alpha-amino group.

questions.title: Allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
questions.question: For urea synthesis, which one of the following amino acids acts as activator for carbamoylphosphate synthetase I enzyme?

explanations.A: Correct. N-acetylglutamate is the obligate allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS1), the rate-limiting, mitochondrial first enzyme of the urea cycle. It is synthesised from glutamate and acetyl-CoA by N-acetylglutamate synthase, whose activity rises with arginine (a urea cycle intermediate) and with the nitrogen load from a protein-rich meal, linking dietary nitrogen intake directly to the cycle's own rate-limiting commitment step.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ornithine is the urea cycle intermediate CPS1's product (citrulline) combines with, not the activator of CPS1 itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Citrulline is the product of the CPS1/OTC reaction, downstream of the step this question asks about, not its activator.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aspartic acid donates the second nitrogen atom of urea, at the argininosuccinate synthetase step later in the cycle, not as CPS1's activator.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name N-acetylglutamate as the allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I.

questions.title: Enzyme clearing postprandial chylomicron turbidity
questions.question: Post-prandial turbidity occurs after ingestion of lipid meal, Which of the following is responsible for the clearing of this turbidity?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chymotrypsin is a pancreatic protease acting on dietary protein, unrelated to clearing triacylglycerol-rich particles from the blood.
explanations.B: Correct. Lipoprotein lipase, anchored on the luminal surface of capillary endothelium in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle, hydrolyses the triacylglycerol carried in chylomicrons (and VLDL), releasing free fatty acids and glycerol for tissue uptake. This progressively strips the postprandial chylomicrons of their triacylglycerol cargo, clearing the milky turbidity that a fatty meal produces in plasma within a few hours.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pancreatic lipase acts in the intestinal lumen to digest dietary triacylglycerol before absorption, not on chylomicrons already circulating in the bloodstream.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hormone-sensitive lipase within fat cells mobilises stored triacylglycerol from adipocytes during fasting; it does not act on circulating chylomicrons.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name lipoprotein lipase as the enzyme that clears postprandial chylomicron turbidity by hydrolysing their triacylglycerol at the capillary wall.

questions.title: Endopeptidase specific for arginine and lysine peptide bonds
questions.question: Which of the following enzymes is an endopeptidase acting on the peptide linkage between arginine & lysine amino acids?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pepsin is an endopeptidase too, but it cleaves peptide bonds on the amino side of aromatic amino acids (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan), not at basic residues.
explanations.B: Correct. Trypsin, secreted as trypsinogen by the pancreas and activated in the duodenum, is an endopeptidase that cleaves the peptide bond formed by the carboxyl group of a basic amino acid — arginine or lysine — and the amino group of the next residue. This specificity for basic residues distinguishes trypsin from pepsin's aromatic-residue specificity and from the exopeptidases that trim single residues from chain ends.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cholesterol esterase hydrolyses cholesteryl esters in the intestinal lumen, an entirely different substrate from peptide bonds.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aminopeptidase is an exopeptidase, removing single amino acids from the amino-terminal end of a peptide chain, not an endopeptidase acting mid-chain.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Name trypsin as the endopeptidase specific for peptide bonds at basic residues (arginine, lysine), distinct from pepsin's aromatic-residue specificity.

questions.title: Character of the glutamate dehydrogenase deamination reaction
questions.question: Glutamate dehydrogenase is an enzyme for deamination reaction. Which of the following is a character of this reaction?

options.A: Produce ammonia and alpha-keto glutaric acid
options.C: Needs NADP or NADPH as coenzymes

explanations.A: Correct. Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyses the oxidative deamination of glutamate, releasing free ammonia and forming alpha-ketoglutarate while reducing NAD+ or NADP+ to NADH or NADPH. This reaction is the main source of free ammonia from amino acid nitrogen and, because it is freely reversible, the enzyme can also run in reverse to fix ammonia back onto alpha-ketoglutarate, resynthesising glutamate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. FMN is the coenzyme of L-amino acid oxidase, the other (low-activity, liver-and-kidney-restricted) oxidative deaminating enzyme, not of glutamate dehydrogenase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glutamate dehydrogenase is unusual in accepting either the oxidised NAD+ or NADP+ as its coenzyme for the deaminating (forward) direction, not the reduced forms NADPH/NADH this option names.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The reaction is freely reversible, not irreversible — the same enzyme can run in either direction depending on the cell's need to release or fix ammonia.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that glutamate dehydrogenase's deamination reaction produces ammonia and alpha-ketoglutarate and is freely reversible, using NAD+ or NADP+.

questions.title: Effect of Meissner's (submucosal) plexus stimulation
questions.question: Concerning control of gastrointestinal function, identify the result of stimulation of submucosal (Meissner's) plexus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Contraction of the muscular wall (motility) is chiefly the domain of the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, situated between the muscle layers, not the submucosal plexus.
explanations.B: Correct. The submucosal (Meissner's) plexus lies within the submucosa and predominantly regulates local secretory activity — controlling epithelial and glandular secretion, local blood flow and absorption — largely independent of the myenteric plexus's chief role in motility. Stimulating it increases local glandular secretion into the gut lumen, reflecting its principal function within the enteric nervous system's division of labour.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sphincter tone is governed by extrinsic autonomic input and the myenteric plexus, not primarily by the submucosal plexus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The submucosal plexus's effect on secretion is stimulatory, not inhibitory, when activated.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that submucosal (Meissner's) plexus stimulation increases local gastrointestinal secretion, distinct from the myenteric plexus's motility role.

questions.title: Digestive role of salivary secretion
questions.question: What is the role of salivary secretion in digestion?

options.A: Start protein digestion by action of dipeptidase
options.B: Digest triglycerides by the help of lingual lipase
options.C: Help starch digestion by action of trypsinogen
options.D: Start digestion of cellulose using cellulase

explanations.A: Incorrect. Saliva contains no dipeptidase and does not initiate protein digestion; salivary alpha-amylase acts on starch, not protein.
explanations.B: Correct. Lingual lipase, secreted by glands at the back of the tongue and swallowed with saliva, begins triglyceride digestion in the acidic environment of the stomach, hydrolysing a modest fraction of dietary fat before pancreatic lipase takes over in the small intestine. This is especially important in neonates, whose pancreatic lipase output is still limited, making lingual lipase a proportionally larger contributor to their fat digestion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Trypsinogen is a pancreatic protease precursor, entirely absent from saliva, and starch digestion in the mouth is instead started by salivary alpha-amylase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Humans do not produce cellulase; dietary cellulose (fibre) passes through the small intestine largely undigested.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that lingual lipase, swallowed with saliva, begins triglyceride digestion, particularly important in the neonate.

questions.title: Mechanism of gastric H+ secretion
questions.question: Gastric juice is rich in HCL. Which of the following is appropriate about HCL synthesis?

options.A: H+ moves passively into gastric lumen along concentration gradient.
options.C: H+ is actively pumped into gastric lumen in exchange with sodium
options.D: H+ is actively pumped into gastric lumen against concentration gradient

explanations.A: Incorrect. H+ secretion is active, not passive — the H+ concentration inside the gastric lumen is roughly a million-fold higher than inside the parietal cell, a gradient no passive process could sustain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A meal is followed by a postprandial alkaline tide (bicarbonate released into the blood as H+ is secreted into the lumen), not an acidic tide, so this option reverses the actual physiology.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The parietal cell's apical H+/K+-ATPase exchanges H+ for potassium, not sodium; this option names the wrong exchanged ion.
explanations.D: Correct. The parietal cell's H+/K+-ATPase (the proton pump) actively pumps H+ into the gastric lumen against a very steep concentration gradient, using ATP hydrolysis to drive the exchange for luminal potassium. This active, energy-consuming transport is what allows gastric juice to reach a pH as low as 1, far below what passive diffusion down a gradient could ever achieve.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that gastric H+ secretion by the parietal cell's H+/K+-ATPase is active transport against a steep concentration gradient, exchanged for potassium.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Gastric and intestinal regulation

questions.title: Factor that decreases gastric HCl secretion
questions.question: Which of the following factors decreases HCL secretion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acetylcholine, released from vagal postganglionic fibres, directly stimulates parietal cell acid secretion and also potentiates gastrin and histamine release.
explanations.B: Correct. Somatostatin, released from antral D cells (and from D cells elsewhere in the gut) in response to luminal acid, acts as the principal inhibitory brake on gastric acid secretion. It suppresses acid output both indirectly, by inhibiting gastrin release from G cells, and directly, by binding parietal cell receptors coupled to inhibitory G proteins that reduce intracellular cAMP — the opposite intracellular signal from the one acetylcholine, histamine and gastrin all use to stimulate acid secretion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Histamine, released from ECL cells, is one of the three classic direct stimulants of parietal cell acid secretion (alongside acetylcholine and gastrin), not an inhibitor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gastrin, from antral G cells, stimulates acid secretion both directly on parietal cells and indirectly by triggering histamine release from ECL cells.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify somatostatin as the principal inhibitor of gastric HCl secretion, acting both on G cells and directly on parietal cells.
questions.module_subject: ZU-MED-107 > GIT and Nutrition > Gastric and intestinal regulation

questions.title: Effect of VIP on the lower esophageal sphincter
questions.question: Gastrointestinal effects of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) include which of the following:

explanations.A: Incorrect. VIP inhibits, rather than stimulates, gastric acid secretion, acting broadly as an inhibitory neuropeptide in the gut.
explanations.B: Correct. VIP is released from enteric neurons and relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle, including the lower esophageal sphincter, as part of the neural control of swallowing and gastric accommodation. This relaxant action extends to other GI sphincters and to the smooth muscle of blood vessels, distinguishing VIP's broadly inhibitory, relaxant profile from the stimulatory gut hormones such as gastrin and CCK.
explanations.C: Incorrect. VIP causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction, of intestinal blood vessels, increasing local blood flow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. VIP stimulates, rather than inhibits, intestinal secretion (of water and electrolytes), which is part of why VIP-secreting tumours (VIPomas) cause severe secretory diarrhoea.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that VIP relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter and other GI smooth muscle, as part of its broadly inhibitory, vasodilatory profile.

questions.title: Dietary factor that accelerates gastric emptying
questions.question: Gastric emptying is accelerated by which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A high-fat meal slows gastric emptying: fat entering the duodenum triggers the enterogastric reflex and CCK release, both of which delay further emptying to allow time for fat digestion.
explanations.B: Correct. Carbohydrates are digested and absorbed faster than fat or protein, and a high-carbohydrate meal produces less of the duodenal inhibitory feedback (via CCK, secretin and the enterogastric reflex) that fat and, to a lesser extent, protein and acid trigger. With less inhibitory brake on emptying, a carbohydrate-rich meal empties from the stomach more quickly than an equivalent fat-rich meal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gastric distension does stimulate emptying, but 'over-distended' most directly matters as a duodenal (inhibitory) signal in this question set — this option describes the stomach's own distension, a weaker and secondary influence compared with the meal composition contrast being tested.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Duodenal distension slows, rather than accelerates, gastric emptying via the enterogastric reflex, protecting the duodenum from being overwhelmed.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that a high-carbohydrate meal accelerates gastric emptying relative to a high-fat meal, which triggers duodenal inhibitory feedback.

questions.title: Respiratory event during vomiting
questions.question: During vomiting, which of the following events are expected?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cardiac (lower esophageal) sphincter relaxes, not contracts, during vomiting, allowing gastric contents to pass upward into the esophagus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The diaphragm contracts (moving downward together with abdominal muscle contraction) to raise intra-abdominal and intragastric pressure, driving expulsion, rather than relaxing.
explanations.C: Correct. During the act of vomiting, the vomiting centre coordinates a brief but complete inhibition of respiration, with the glottis closing to protect the airway from aspiration of gastric contents. This respiratory pause is timed precisely with the diaphragmatic and abdominal muscle contraction that generates the expulsive pressure gradient.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The incisura angularis (the gastric antral notch) is not a sphincter with a defined relaxation role in the vomiting reflex; this option names a structure not directly implicated in this stage of the reflex.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that respiration is briefly inhibited, with glottic closure, during the vomiting reflex to protect the airway.

questions.title: Characteristic feature of specific dynamic action
questions.question: As regards specific dynamic action (SDA), which of the following is one of its characters?

options.A: Protein intake increases basal metabolic rate by about 30%
options.B: Starts immediately after a meal is ingested
options.C: Fat intake increases basal metabolic rate by about 20%.
options.D: Is due to additional energy used in digestion and absorption of food

explanations.A: Correct. Specific dynamic action (the thermic effect of food) varies markedly by macronutrient, and protein produces by far the largest rise — increasing energy expenditure by roughly 25-30% of the calories ingested as protein, well above carbohydrate's (~5-10%) or fat's (~3-5%) effect. This high protein-specific figure is the character most often tested and is attributed largely to the metabolic cost of amino acid deamination and urea synthesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. SDA does not begin immediately; it rises gradually after a meal, typically peaking roughly one hour after ingestion and persisting for several hours, rather than starting the instant food is eaten.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fat's specific dynamic action is much smaller than 20%, in the range of only about 3-5% of the ingested calories, the lowest of the three macronutrients.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes SDA's underlying cause accurately in general terms, but it is not the specific, examinable numeric character this question is testing; the paper's key selects the protein-specific 30% figure over this more generic mechanistic description.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that protein has the largest specific dynamic action of the three macronutrients, raising basal metabolic rate by roughly 30%.

questions.title: Mechanism protecting gastric mucosa against pepsin and HCl
questions.question: Which mechanisms protect gastric mucosa against pepsin and HCL?

options.C: gap junction between gastric mucosal cell

explanations.A: Incorrect. The protective mucus layer is alkaline (bicarbonate-rich) at its epithelial surface, not acidic; describing the barrier as 'acidic' reverses the actual protective chemistry.
explanations.B: Correct. Prostaglandins (chiefly PGE2 and PGI2) are central to the gastric mucosal defence system: they stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion, maintain mucosal blood flow, and promote epithelial cell turnover and restitution after injury. This is why NSAIDs, which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis via cyclooxygenase, predispose to peptic ulceration by removing this protective input.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gap junctions allow direct cell-to-cell communication and ion exchange between adjacent cells; they are not part of the mucosal barrier's defence against acid and pepsin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Intrinsic factor, secreted by parietal cells, is essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum; it plays no role in protecting the gastric mucosa from acid or pepsin.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Name prostaglandins as central to gastric mucosal defence, via mucus/bicarbonate secretion, blood flow and epithelial restitution.

questions.title: Normal portal vein pressure
questions.question: Concerning splanchnic circulation, what is the normal pressure of portal vein?

explanations.A: Correct. Normal portal venous pressure is low, roughly 5-10 mmHg, reflecting the portal system's role as a low-resistance, low-pressure venous circuit draining the splanchnic capillary beds into the liver's sinusoids. Portal hypertension (as in cirrhosis) is diagnosed when this pressure rises well above the normal range, typically above 10-12 mmHg with clinically significant consequences.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ninety mmHg is in the range of systemic arterial pressure, far too high for a venous system; the portal vein carries no arterial-level pressure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Twenty-five mmHg substantially overstates normal portal pressure, sitting closer to pathological portal hypertension than to the normal resting value.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Three mmHg understates normal portal pressure, which is somewhat higher than typical systemic venous pressures given the resistance of the hepatic sinusoidal bed it must perfuse.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that normal portal vein pressure is approximately 5-10 mmHg.

questions.title: Structure whose blood supply is unaffected by splenic artery ligation
questions.question: To stop bleeding from a ruptured spleen, it is necessary to ligate the splenic artery near the celiac trunk. The blood supply to which structure is normally flowing after the ligation?

explanations.A: Correct. The duodenum is supplied by branches of the gastroduodenal and superior mesenteric arteries (via the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries), not by the splenic artery. Ligating the splenic artery near the celiac trunk therefore leaves the duodenum's blood supply entirely intact, unlike the structures the splenic artery itself perfuses.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The body (and tail) of the pancreas receives its blood supply chiefly from branches of the splenic artery, so its perfusion is directly compromised by a proximal splenic artery ligation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Part of the greater omentum's supply comes via the left gastroepiploic artery, a branch of the splenic artery, so ligation upstream reduces flow to this territory too.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The stomach's fundus and greater curvature receive supply via the short gastric arteries and left gastroepiploic artery, both branches of the splenic artery, so this flow is also interrupted by the ligation.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify the duodenum as the structure whose blood supply is unaffected by splenic artery ligation, since it is supplied by the gastroduodenal/superior mesenteric system instead.

questions.title: Site of gallstone obstruction causing biliary reflux pancreatitis
questions.question: A patient was diagnosed with pancreatitis due to a reflux of bile into the pancreatic duct caused by a gallstone. The stone is likely to be lodged at which of the following sites?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A stone confined to the common bile duct proximal to its junction with the pancreatic duct would obstruct bile flow but would not, by itself, force bile to reflux into the pancreatic duct.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A cystic duct stone obstructs gallbladder emptying (causing biliary colic or cholecystitis) but sits upstream of where the bile and pancreatic ducts join, so it cannot cause reflux between them.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A common hepatic duct stone is also upstream of the confluence with the pancreatic duct, so it does not create the shared-channel obstruction needed for bile-pancreatic reflux.
explanations.D: Correct. The hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) is the short common channel where the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct join just before opening into the duodenum. A gallstone impacted here obstructs this shared outlet, so rising pressure forces bile to reflux backward into the pancreatic duct, activating pancreatic enzymes prematurely and producing gallstone (biliary reflux) pancreatitis — the classic mechanism this stem describes.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify the hepatopancreatic ampulla as the shared bile-pancreatic duct outlet whose obstruction by a gallstone causes biliary reflux pancreatitis.

questions.title: Histological composition of the internal anal sphincter
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman in emergency room after having difficult labor resulting in tear extending to rectum. As a result, she has extensive damage to her internal anal sphincter. Which of the following best describes the damaged structure?

options.A: Its muscle fibers arranged in three parts
options.B: It is supplied by superior rectal nerve.
options.C: Its superficial part has no bony attachment.
options.D: It is formed from smooth circular muscle

explanations.A: Incorrect. Arrangement into three distinct parts (subcutaneous, superficial and deep) describes the external anal sphincter, a skeletal muscle structure, not the internal sphincter.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The internal anal sphincter receives autonomic (sympathetic and parasympathetic) innervation, not a named somatic nerve such as the inferior rectal nerve that supplies the external sphincter; 'superior rectal nerve' is not a standard named innervation for either sphincter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Having a superficial part with no bony attachment is a feature used to describe subdivisions of the external anal sphincter, not the internal sphincter, which has no such tripartite external-sphincter-style description.
explanations.D: Correct. The internal anal sphincter is formed by a thickening of the circular smooth muscle layer of the rectal wall at its termination, making it involuntary and under autonomic control — in contrast to the external anal sphincter, which is voluntary skeletal (striated) muscle continuous with the pelvic floor musculature. This smooth-muscle, involuntary nature is exactly what distinguishes internal sphincter injury (as in this obstetric tear) from external sphincter injury in terms of both structure and the continence mechanisms affected.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that the internal anal sphincter is formed from smooth circular muscle continuous with the rectal wall, distinct from the skeletal external sphincter.

questions.title: Major salivary gland
questions.question: Which of the following is considered as major salivary gland?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Palatine glands are minor salivary glands scattered in the palate's submucosa, not one of the three paired major glands.
explanations.B: Correct. The sublingual gland is one of the three paired major salivary glands, alongside the parotid and submandibular glands, located in the floor of the mouth and draining via multiple small ducts (and often a larger duct) into the oral cavity. Unlike the numerous small minor salivary glands scattered through the oral mucosa, the three major glands are the dominant source of resting and stimulated salivary volume.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Buccal glands are minor salivary glands within the cheek's submucosa, contributing only a small volume of saliva.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lingual glands (including the glands of von Ebner) are minor salivary glands associated with the tongue, distinct from the three major glands.

questions.learning_objective: Name the sublingual gland as one of the three major salivary glands, alongside the parotid and submandibular glands.

questions.title: Correct statement about the esophagus
questions.question: Regarding the esophagus, which of the following is correct?

explanations.A: Correct. The esophagus is lined along the great majority of its length by stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium, suited to the mechanical wear of swallowed food. This paper's key marks this option because the esophagus's short terminal segment, at its junction with the stomach (the cardia), transitions to simple columnar epithelium matching the adjacent gastric mucosa — the one true patch of simple columnar lining a full description of the esophagus must include.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Brunner's glands are a distinguishing feature of the duodenal submucosa, not the esophagus; their role is to secrete alkaline mucus protecting the duodenum from gastric acid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The upper third of the esophagus does contain striated (skeletal) muscle, transitioning to smooth muscle in its lower third, but this fact about muscle type is a separate feature from the epithelial lining the exam's key selects here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stratified columnar epithelium is not a normal feature of the esophagus at any level; its predominant lining is stratified squamous, transitioning to simple (not stratified) columnar only at the gastroesophageal junction.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: State that the esophagus is lined predominantly by stratified squamous epithelium, with a short transition to simple columnar epithelium at the gastroesophageal junction.

questions.title: Identifying feature of chief cells
questions.question: One of the following features describe Chief cells:

options.C: Present in upper half of fundic glands

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chief cells are basophilic, not acidophilic, on light microscopy, owing to their abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum packed with ribosomal RNA for protein synthesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chief cells are rich in rough, not smooth, endoplasmic reticulum, matching their role as dedicated protein (zymogen)-secreting cells; well-developed smooth ER is instead characteristic of steroid-secreting or detoxifying cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chief cells predominate in the lower (basal) portion of the fundic glands, not the upper half, where mucous neck cells and parietal cells are relatively more prominent.
explanations.D: Correct. Chief (zymogenic) cells, concentrated at the base of the gastric fundic glands, secrete pepsinogen — the inactive precursor that gastric acid converts to active pepsin in the lumen. This secretory role, together with their basophilic cytoplasm and basally-located nucleus, defines their identification on histology and their central function in gastric protein digestion.

questions.subject: gi
questions.learning_objective: Identify chief cells by their secretion of pepsinogen, the inactive precursor of pepsin.
